glossary.def: A speaker's/signer's judgment about whether a form is possible in their language; an empirical observation used as data. Also called a grammaticality judgment.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The property that, for most words, the pairing between a word's form and its meaning is conventional rather than inherent (e.g., 'pumpkin' vs. Nishnaabemwin 'kosmaan').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Knowledge of how the articulators (mouth, tongue, lips; or hands, fingers, wrists) are used to produce the sounds or signs of a language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A term that is secretly derogatory only to those with in-group knowledge (e.g., 'Monday' used as a coded racial slur) — derogatory without necessarily causing offense to the unaware target.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A large database collecting real examples of language use (books, newspapers, message boards, video, audio) used as a tool for making observations.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Using a trans person's former (pre-transition) name, whether accidentally or deliberately; a way names are used to enforce power.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Harm in which a linguistic expression disparages people; expresses the utterer's condemnation of a referent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Describing expressions that disparage people. Offense (impact on hearers) and derogation (utterer's attitude) are distinct: an expression can be one, both, or neither.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Describing what people actually do with their language, without judging it — the goal of scientific linguistics.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Based on systematic observation of data as evidence for theories.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: An expression used for emotional outbursts (e.g., damn). An expression can be both a vulgarity and an expletive.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A language learned from the people around you in early childhood; a person may have more than one L1. (Contrast with L2, introduced in Ch. 2.)
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: In linguistics, the mental system of knowledge underlying a language — not a book of 'proper-usage' rules. Every human language has a grammar.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Whether a form could be generated by the mental grammar of a language. 'Ungrammatical' (marked with *) means the grammar cannot produce it — about what is possible, not merely what exists.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: In a matched-guise study, the varying label or presentation applied to the stimulus (e.g., the name on a résumé, an accent, a face shown with a voice).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Unconscious knowledge a fluent user has about their language that they cannot easily articulate (contrast: explicit knowledge).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Replacing or mispronouncing someone's name to make it 'sound more English/white,' stripping their connection to family, community, and language (Bucholtz).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Governmental/institutional rules that encourage or force the use (or non-use) of languages, require proficiency, or regulate languages in public space — usable to erase OR reinforce identities.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A program trained on a vast corpus that calculates the probability that pieces of language relate to one another, used to generate statistically plausible text; it has no mind or communicative intent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The 'killing' of a language through policy (e.g., residential-school prohibitions on Indigenous languages).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Judgments people (including linguists) make about others based on how they use language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The scientific study of human language: describing the patterns of languages and drawing conclusions about the shared systems in speakers' and signers' minds.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A technique for revealing hidden attitudes: hold a STIMULUS constant and vary its GUISE; any difference in participant ratings is attributed to the guise, not the stimulus.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The shared cognitive system in a language user's mind that lets them produce and understand a language and be understood by others who know it.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The part of the grammar that links forms (sounds, signs, or symbols) to meanings — a kind of dictionary in the mind.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Conscious knowledge you have about your grammar, as distinct from the (often unconscious) grammatical knowledge itself.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The physical channel of a language: whether it is vocalized (spoken) or signed.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The part of grammar dealing with the meaningful pieces inside words and how they combine (e.g., adding -s to make a plural).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A sequence of N items occurring in a given order in a corpus (bigram = 2, trigram = 3), used to model co-occurrence probabilities.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Social/psychological harm done to discourse participants (hearers/viewers) by an expression in a given context; can occur regardless of the speaker's intent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The view that vocal language is more important than signed language — a bias that has caused harm to deaf people and to the study of sign languages.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A derogatory term (jerk, idiot, asshole; also called a general pejorative) condemning a specific person for specific behavior, rather than an entire group.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Improved comprehension of an unfamiliar talker or accent as a result of more listening experience; extends across speakers and even across different accents.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: An utterance that not only conveys information but performs an action that changes reality (e.g., 'I concede,' 'I now pronounce you married') — provided the right authority, sincerity, and audience uptake exist.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The property of language by which utterances (and other social practices) can perform actions and affect reality, including constructing identity (Austin; extended by Butler).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The area of grammar concerned with the physical production and perception of the sounds or signs of language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The part of grammar governing how the physical units of a language can be combined and how they change in different contexts.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The part of grammar concerned with how meaning arises in context (e.g., how 'I have some news' can be read as good or bad).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Prescribing how people should or should not use language (e.g., style-guide 'rules'). Not the goal of linguistics.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The social value attached to a language variety; higher-prestige forms are often those used by more powerful or privileged groups, not objectively superior ones.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The property that a language can produce an infinite number of new words and sentences from a finite vocabulary and finite set of combining principles. Also called creativity.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Repurposing a slur as a marker of shared identity and solidarity against oppression (e.g., 'queer'); not all targeted members may be ready to embrace a reclaimed term.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Any language learned after one already has an L1 (even if it is one's third or fourth language). One's L2 accent is shaped by the phonology of one's L1.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The part of grammar that calculates the meanings of words, phrases, and sentences; works together with syntax.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: An insult that denigrates a specific marginalized group; targets a person BECAUSE of group membership. Power imbalance is essential — insults aimed at high-status groups lack the same force.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Use of 'they/them' to refer to a single, known individual (e.g., 'Samnang told me they needed an extension'); an in-progress grammatical change resisted by prescriptivists.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The variety of a language that most closely matches dictionaries, textbooks, and high-status media; its status comes from social/economic/political power, not from being linguistically 'better.'
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Negative attitudes and expectations attached to a non-standard accent or variety (the variety itself is neither good nor bad); can cause real harm in jobs, housing, courts, and education.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: In a matched-guise study, the element held constant across conditions (e.g., the résumé, the sales script, the recorded voice).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The part of grammar that determines how words can and cannot be combined into phrases and sentences.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A word or expression whose use is avoided except in certain circumstances; using it in the wrong context breaks the taboo and causes offence. Taboos can arise for negative OR positive (respect) reasons.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A strategy of replacing a taboo word with another word — either to avoid resembling it (e.g., Kambaata in-law names) or to evoke it via a similar form (e.g., 'sugar,' 'shoot' for a swear).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: In an LLM, a unit of language — a letter, word, piece of a word (morpheme), or punctuation mark — whose co-occurrence probabilities are calculated.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The especially offensive emotional power of slurs, arising from the power differential and the invocation of historical violence against the targeted group; so strong that even mentioning some slurs can cause harm.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The difference between USING a word to refer to something in the world vs. MENTIONING the word itself as a linguistic object (conventionally shown in italics).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A voice quality produced by very low-frequency vocal-fold vibration, sounding creaky; a normal part of many languages' phonetics/prosody, disproportionately criticized in women's voices.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: An expression involving taboo bodily references (e.g., shit, ass).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: The scientific (descriptive, empirical) study of human language and the shared mental systems behind it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: The shared system in users' minds that lets them understand and be understood — not prescriptive 'rules.'
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Name the components of mental grammar.
flashcards.back: Phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics (plus the mental lexicon).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: Descriptive = describe what users actually do; prescriptive = dictate what they 'should' do. Linguistics is descriptive.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: An ungrammatical form — one the mental grammar cannot generate (e.g., *'lbitfer').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: Arbitrariness — the pairing is conventional, not inherent (with some iconic exceptions).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: A finite vocabulary + finite rules can generate infinitely many new words and sentences.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: Whether it is vocalized (spoken) or signed.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Is reading/writing part of core mental grammar?
flashcards.back: No — it's a secondary skill; users have full grammars without literacy, and some languages have no written form.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: Conscious knowledge about your grammar, vs. the unconscious grammatical knowledge itself.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Three accessible tools of language science?
flashcards.back: Acceptability judgments, surveys, and corpora (plus experiments, phonetic software, neuroimaging).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.back: By combining tokens in statistically probable sequences from training data — combinatorial, with no meaning or intent of its own.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Human language vs. LLM output — key difference?
flashcards.back: Human language is generative and shared to communicate meaning; LLM output is combinatorial with no communicative intention.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What is a performative speech act?
flashcards.back: An utterance that performs an action and changes reality (e.g., 'I now pronounce you married'), given proper authority, sincerity, and audience uptake.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: J. L. Austin ('How to Do Things With Words') and Judith Butler (who extended it to gender/identity).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Offense = harm to the hearers/viewers (impact); derogation = the utterer's disparaging attitude. An expression can be one, both, or neither.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Vulgarity = taboo bodily reference (shit, ass); expletive = outburst term (damn). Some words are both.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: What makes something a slur (vs. a particularistic insult)?
flashcards.back: A slur denigrates a whole marginalized GROUP and depends on a power imbalance; a particularistic insult condemns one person for specific behavior.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Their emotional power comes from a power differential and the invocation of historical violence — even mentioning some can harm.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Using a word refers to a thing; mentioning a word treats the word itself as a linguistic object (shown in italics).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: How does a matched-guise study work?
flashcards.back: Hold the STIMULUS constant, vary the GUISE; any rating difference is due to the guise (the label), revealing hidden attitudes.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: In the résumé study, what were stimulus and guise?
flashcards.back: Stimulus = the (constant) résumé; guise = the name at the top (English- vs. non-English-sounding).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Replacing/mispronouncing a name to make it 'sound more English/white,' erasing identity (Bucholtz).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: Unspecified singular 'they' is ~600 years old; the NEW change is SPECIFIC singular 'they' for a known person.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Can anyone stop language from changing?
flashcards.back: No. Language change is inevitable; prescriptive complaints don't stop it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.back: The killing of a language through policy (e.g., residential schools forbidding Indigenous languages).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Why do L2 users have accents?
flashcards.back: Their L2 mental grammar is shaped by their L1's phonology; accent 'reduction' is hard after childhood — but comprehension adapts more easily.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: The sentence 'Sam bumped the passenger with the rolling suitcase' has two meanings (Sam had the suitcase vs. the passenger did). Which components of the grammar produce this ambiguity?
options: Syntax and semantics
Phonology
Phonetics
Morphology only
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: Newfoundland English allows 'I eats toast every day' and 'You knows the answer.' Which part of the grammar differs from standardized Canadian English here?
options: Morphology
Syntax
Phonetics
Semantics
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: Which is the best definition of 'mental grammar' as used in this book?
options: A shared cognitive system that lets users understand and be understood
A style guide of correct-usage rules
A dictionary of a language's words
The writing system of a language
questions.answer: A shared cognitive system that lets users understand and be understood
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: Why do LLMs sometimes produce different sentences for the same prompt?
options: They sample among several high-probability tokens instead of always the top one
They understand the user's intent differently each time
They randomly ignore their training data
They have their own opinions
questions.answer: They sample among several high-probability tokens instead of always the top one
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: True or False: If everyone spoke standardized English, we could eliminate all language bias.
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: True or False: Studying linguistics will make your grammar 'better.'
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: True or False: An LLM has a mental representation of the meaning of the words it outputs.
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: True or False: Reading and writing are core, necessary parts of a person's mental grammar.
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: The property by which a finite vocabulary and finite set of rules can produce an infinite number of new sentences is called ____ (also called generativity or creativity).
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: An approach that DESCRIBES what speakers actually do (rather than dictating what they should do) is called a ____ approach.
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

questions.text: In an LLM, the units whose co-occurrence probabilities are calculated — letters, words, morphemes, or punctuation — are called ____.

pairs.right: Large database of real language use

questions.text: How recently has 'they' been used as a SINGULAR pronoun in English?
options: It has been a generic singular for centuries and is now also changing to a specific singular
It started being used as a singular around 2015
Never — 'they' is always plural
Only since the Merriam-Webster 2019 vote
questions.answer: It has been a generic singular for centuries and is now also changing to a specific singular
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: How can people stop a language from 'deteriorating'?
options: No one can stop language from changing
Teach only correct grammar in schools
Correct every mistake people make
Publish and distribute extensive dictionaries
questions.answer: No one can stop language from changing
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: In a study where the same sales script was spoken with either a standardized American accent or a Greek accent, which is true?
options: The script is the stimulus and the accent is the guise
The product is the stimulus and the accent is the guise
The accent is the stimulus and the product is the guise
The script is the guise and the accent is the stimulus
questions.answer: The script is the stimulus and the accent is the guise
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: Identical résumés were sent under English, Indian, or Chinese names and callbacks were measured. Which is true?
options: The job-seeker's name is the guise and the résumé is the stimulus
The résumé is the guise and the interview is the stimulus
The name is the stimulus and the interview is the guise
The hiring manager is the guise and the résumé is the stimulus
questions.answer: The job-seeker's name is the guise and the résumé is the stimulus
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: Which best distinguishes a SLUR from a particularistic insult?
options: A slur targets a whole marginalized group and depends on a power imbalance
A slur is simply any rude word
A slur only targets one person's specific behavior
A slur is always less harmful than an insult
questions.answer: A slur targets a whole marginalized group and depends on a power imbalance
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: True or False: 'Offense' and 'derogation' are the same thing.
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: True or False: A performative speech act like 'I now pronounce you married' changes the world regardless of who says it or in what context.

questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

questions.text: True or False: Because power imbalance is essential to a slur, an insult aimed at a high-status group carries the same toxic force as a slur.
questions.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 2
notes.body: ★ PERFORMATIVE speech acts DO things (Austin); Butler extends performativity to IDENTITY. Power needs authority + sincerity + uptake. ★ TABOO words are context-avoided; violating them causes OFFENSE. Taboos can be positive (respect) or negative. ★ OFFENSE = harm to hearers (impact); DEROGATION = utterer's disparaging attitude — INDEPENDENT of each other. ★ VULGARITY (bodily: shit) vs. EXPLETIVE (outburst: damn). ★ PARTICULARISTIC INSULT = one person for behavior; SLUR = a whole marginalized GROUP + POWER IMBALANCE → TOXICITY; slurs can be RECLAIMED (queer). ★ USE (refer) vs. MENTION (word as object, italics). ★ MATCHED-GUISE: hold STIMULUS constant, vary GUISE → rating difference = attitude toward the guise. ★ INDEXICAL BLEACHING = making a name 'sound more white'; DEADNAMING enforces power. ★ SPECIFIC singular 'they' = new change (unspecified singular they is ~600 yrs old); no one can stop language change. ★ VOCAL FRY/creak = normal phonation, policed in women. ★ STIGMA attaches to non-standard accents (accent itself is neutral); L2 accent shaped by L1; fix via PERCEPTUAL ADAPTATION. ★ LANGUAGE POLICY can erase or reinforce identity; residential-school prohibition = LINGUICIDE; Official Languages Act 1969 (FR/EN) ignored Indigenous languages; Indigenous Languages Act 2019.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.8 Exercise your linguistics skills
notes.body: Practice: (1) use morphology to compare 'standardized' vs. 'standard language' (what does -ize add, and why choose one term?); (2) reflect on feelings about your L2 accent and whether they trace to prestige/power; (3) examine which names/nicknames you use with different groups and why; (4) analyze swearing across contexts in terms of face (is positive or negative face threatened or enhanced?).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.7 Legally enshrined harms
notes.body: Governments use language policy to create unity or division. Canada's Official Languages Act (1969) recognized French and English and helped Francophones, but ignored Indigenous languages. Residential-school policies mandating English/French were a form of linguicide whose harms are ongoing. The 2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission led to the Indigenous Languages Act (2019) supporting reclamation. Tensions remain: Mary Simon (bilingual in English and Inuktitut) was criticized for limited French; Quebec's French-protection laws can suppress Indigenous and other languages (many Cree/Mohawk speakers use English, not French, as their L2).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.6 Linguistic law enforcement
notes.body: Unlike most social differences, deviating from a privileged language standard is openly policed. People police voices — criticizing 'uptalk' and vocal fry (creak), a normal low-frequency phonation disproportionately condemned in women even though men creak equally. People also police accents: a non-standard accent is stigmatized (the accent itself is neutral). L2 accents arise because the L2 grammar is shaped by L1 phonology. Stigma has real consequences (jobs, housing, courts, special-ed streaming, voice assistants). A UBC matched-guise study: the SAME voice was rated as more accented when paired with a Chinese-Canadian face — a mismatch of expectations. Remedy: perceptual adaptation — the more you attend to a talker/accent, the better you understand them.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.5 Pronouns, language change, and the grammar police
notes.body: Pronouns index identity. English third-person singular pronouns (it/he/she) give broad clues (thing/male/female) that can exclude people; 'they' avoids this. Unspecified singular 'they' is ~600 years old; the current change adds SPECIFIC singular 'they' for a known person. Because this tracks changing gender norms, prescriptivists resist it, but it keeps spreading (2015 ADS Word of the Year). A parallel: English lost thou/thee, leaving 'you' for both singular and plural. No one can stop language change, but users can speed it — using specific-singular-'they' reduces harmful misgendering.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.4 The power of names
notes.body: Names index social categories (gender, age, ethnicity). Matched-guise studies reveal hidden attitudes by holding a stimulus constant and varying its guise: identical résumés got fewer callbacks under non-English names (Oreopoulos 2011); Toronto landlords replied less to typically Arabic names. Names express identity and resistance — Indigenous name reclamation (e.g., Ta7talíya Nahanee, whose Sḵwx̱wú7mesh name uses '7' for the glottal stop) and trans naming. Deadnaming, forcible renaming, and mispronunciation enforce power (e.g., Black train porters all called 'George'; NDP leader Jagmeet Singh called 'Juggy'). Bucholtz calls making a name 'sound more English/white' indexical bleaching.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.3 Derogation, toxicity, and power imbalances
notes.body: Language expresses solidarity (e.g., Japanese honorific/endearment suffixes -san, -chan) but also harms. Offense = harm to discourse participants (impact); derogation/pejoration = the utterer's disparaging attitude. These are independent: 'shit' can offend without being derogatory; a coded slur ('Monday') can be derogatory without offending an unaware target. Particularistic insults (general pejoratives: jerk, idiot, asshole) target one person for specific behavior; slurs denigrate a whole marginalized GROUP and depend on a power imbalance, invoking historical violence — this is their toxicity. Insults aimed at high-status groups lack that force. Slurs can be reclaimed for solidarity (e.g., 'queer'; 'suffragette'). [Content note: discusses slurs.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.2 Language and offence
notes.body: Words carry emotional effects. Taboo words are avoided except in certain contexts; violating a taboo causes offence (e.g., 'shit' vs. innocuous 'poop'). Taboos arise for negative reasons OR positive ones (respect — e.g., Kambaata women avoiding sounds in in-laws' names). Taboo avoidance replaces a taboo word, either to avoid resembling it or to evoke it with a similar form ('sugar,' 'shoot'). The use–mention distinction matters: using 'shit' violates the taboo, but mentioning it as a linguistic object (in italics) usually doesn't — though for highly volatile words like racial slurs, even mentions can harm, so people use circumlocution or masking (s***, s-word). [Content note: swearing; brief mention of slurs.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.1 Language and identity (performativity)
notes.body: Language can change the world. Performative speech acts (Austin) both convey information and perform an action ('I concede,' 'I now pronounce you married,' 'you're hired'). Their power depends on the authority and sincerity of the utterer plus the audience's uptake and society's agreement — a kid at recess saying 'I now pronounce you married' changes nothing. Butler extended performativity beyond speech acts: identity (e.g., gender) is a 'performative accomplishment' built through repeated social practice, including language. Saying 'eh' both expresses and reinforces a Canadian identity. Performativity ≠ acting/pretending — it means language performs functions that construct who we are.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: Chapter 2 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 2 you should be able to: (1) describe relationships between power and language across a variety of scenarios; (2) find real-world examples of language–power relationships; and (3) use metalinguistic awareness to interpret your own and others' attitudes about language.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 1
notes.body: ★ Linguistics = scientific, DESCRIPTIVE, EMPIRICAL study of human language. ★ 'Grammar' = the MENTAL system, not a rulebook; every language has one; none is 'better.' ★ Components: phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics (+ mental lexicon). ★ Form–meaning pairing is ARBITRARY (mostly). ★ Productivity/generativity = infinite output from finite means. ★ * marks an UNGRAMMATICAL form; grammaticality = what's POSSIBLE, not what exists. ★ Acceptability/grammaticality judgments are empirical DATA; other tools = surveys, corpora, experiments (Praat/ELAN, EEG, fMRI). ★ Standard = STANDARDIZED variety backed by social power, not linguistic superiority; bias/prestige intersect with race (Black English/AAVE). ★ Language science can do harm (missionary mis-documentation, residential schools, oralism) — practice HUMILITY. ★ LLMs are COMBINATORIAL (predict likely tokens via n-gram intuition/neural nets + RLHF); NO mind or communicative intent — unlike human generative, shared language. ★ Modality = spoken vs. signed; reading/writing are SECONDARY. ★ Implicit knowledge = unconscious grammatical knowledge; metalinguistic awareness = conscious knowledge about it.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.9 Exercise your linguistics skills
notes.body: Practice: (1) identify your L1(s) and make two descriptive (not prescriptive) observations; (2) evaluate invented product names — which are possible English words and why (phonotactic intuition); (3) coin new verbs from nouns/proper names ('Megabussing to Montreal,' 'got Pfizered') to illustrate generativity; (4) find a very new word and write a corpus-based dictionary definition.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.8 How do ChatBots synthesize sentences?
notes.body: LLMs trace back to Shannon (1948) and Markov (1913): the idea of an n-gram — the probability of the next item given previous ones (bigram QU is high-probability; a trigram like 'proud of ___' often predicts 'you'). Items are called tokens (letters, words, morphemes, punctuation). Real LLMs don't use raw n-grams but neural networks of weighted 'perceptrons' that predict likely next tokens. To avoid repetitive output, models sample among high-probability tokens (so outputs vary). After training, models are tuned with guardrails and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) — done by often underpaid, traumatized human labelers. Pronoun defaults (e.g., male doctor / female receptionist) show how training and rating choices bake in bias. Chatbots use 'I'/'you' to feel human, but they are not conversing.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.7 Do ChatBots have language?
notes.body: Human grammar is generative: a mind forms an idea, the body sends a signal, another mind interprets it, and a shared mental grammar makes mutual understanding possible. 'Generative AI' text generation relies on Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on huge corpora (often copyrighted, non-consensually scraped). An LLM has no mind or mental representation; it outputs statistically plausible word strings. Humans then can't help interpreting the output (like pareidolia). Human language is generative and shared to communicate meaning; LLM output is merely combinatorial, with no communicative intent — its 'meaning' is what humans attribute to it.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.6 Doing good with language science
notes.body: Linguistics skills apply widely: speech technology and reducing bias in speech recognition; language-learning apps; supporting Indigenous language reclamation (following community leadership, not as an outside 'saviour'); language teaching/ESL certification; and speech-language pathology (therapy after brain injury, gender-affirming voice work, accent coaching). Linguists also work in forensic linguistics, marketing/branding, authorship identification, and constructed languages for film/TV.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.5 Doing harm with language science
notes.body: Science is not inherently virtuous. Early 'linguistics' by missionaries mis-documented Indigenous languages through a Latin/European lens and 'froze' forms via writing; colonial governments then imposed English/French, including through residential schools where children were forbidden their languages and abused. Modern linguistics can also harm: extracting data without benefit to communities, publishing sensitive material, becoming an outside 'authority,' turning descriptions into prescriptions, and — via oralism — neglecting sign languages and mislabeling difference as 'disorder' (e.g., autistic 'pragmatic deficits' that vanished when autistic people talked with each other). Lesson: approach language science with humility. [Content note: residential schools, abuse.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.4 Standards and 'proper' grammar
notes.body: Everyone has linguistic biases. A 'standard' variety is really the standardized one that matches dictionaries/schools/high-status media, and its status comes from social power (e.g., the Académie Française; 'the Queen's English'), not linguistic superiority. Prestige and bias intersect with race: Standard American English implicitly means 'the way white people speak,' excluding varieties like Black English (AAL/AAVE). Treating the standardized form as the only 'correct' one discriminates against users of other varieties (examples: Kreyòl-speaking kids taught only in French; a judge distrusting a Nigerian-accented doctor).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.3 Studying language scientifically
notes.body: Doing linguistics scientifically means making systematic, empirical observations and taking a descriptive (not prescriptive) approach. A key tool is metalinguistic awareness — accessing conscious knowledge about your grammar. Acceptability/grammaticality judgments are empirical data: e.g., 'What did Sam compare the forged painting with?' is grammatical, but *'…and?' is not (marked with *). Other tools: surveys (regional variation, e.g., hoodie/bunny hug), corpora (large databases of real usage), specialized software (Praat, ELAN), and experiments (reaction times, eye-tracking, EEG, fMRI).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.2 What grammars are and aren't
notes.body: 'Grammar' here means the mental system, not a rulebook. Every language has a grammar; claiming a language 'has no grammar' is a racist/colonialist/ableist move. No grammar, dialect, or variety is linguistically better than another — scientists describe, they don't rank. A core property is creativity/productivity/generativity: finite words + finite principles yield infinitely many sentences. Because grammar is productive, languages always change; complaints that young people 'ruin' a language are perennial and unfounded.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.1 What even is language?
notes.body: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language. The word 'language' has several senses; linguistics focuses on human languages (spoken or signed), not computer or metaphorical 'languages.' Successful communication implies a shared system — the mental grammar. Its parts: the mental lexicon links forms to meanings (mostly an arbitrary pairing); articulatory phonetics governs producing sounds/signs; phonology governs how units combine and change; morphology handles meaningful pieces inside words; syntax combines words into phrases/sentences; semantics computes meaning; pragmatics handles meaning in context. Much grammatical knowledge is implicit (unconscious). Reading and writing are secondary — many languages and users have full grammars without literacy.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: Chapter 1 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 1 you should be able to: (1) differentiate prescriptive vs. descriptive ways of thinking about language; (2) identify the components of mental grammar; (3) explain properties shared by all human languages; (4) describe techniques for doing language science; and (5) discuss the ethics of doing language science.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]
